title_en: Dialogue on Religion and Secularism - Episode 5
description_en: The Review Program on Al-Iraqiya Satellite Channel - with Sa'dun Damad
summary: In this fifth episode of the dialogue on religion and secularism, Sayyid Kamal al-Haydari addresses the critical issue of excommunication (takfir) and sectarian violence within the Islamic heritage. He argues that both Sunni and Shi'i schools of thought have historically developed theological and jurisprudential frameworks that declare the other to be unbelievers (kuffar) or even polytheists (mushrikin) based on their respective readings of the Imamate and political legitimacy. Al-Haydari traces this problem to two roots: an epistemological root, where each group claims to possess absolute truth, and a textual root, which relies heavily on fabricated and problematic hadith narrations rather than the Qur'an. He critiques the traditional seminary (hawza) stance that leaves the application of takfir to laypeople, which has historically led to bloodshed. To resolve this, al-Haydari advocates for a fundamental revision of religious readings, emphasizing that no single human interpretation represents the absolute divine truth, and that the Qur'an establishes difference as a means for mutual recognition and integration rather than conflict.
key_points: The issue of excommunication (takfir) and sectarian violence is deeply rooted in the historical readings of both Sunni and Shi'i schools.
Sunni jurisprudence historically declared those who deny the necessity of the early caliphs' legitimacy to be unbelievers, as cited from al-Qurtubi's Al-Mufhim.

Shi'i scholars historically viewed the Imamate as a fundamental root (asl) of religion, leading to the consensus that those who deny it are inwardly unbelievers, as cited from al-Shaykh al-Mufid, al-'Allama al-Hilli, al-Majlisi, and Ayatollah al-Khoei.
The epistemological root of sectarian conflict is the dogmatic belief by each sect that it possesses the absolute truth.
The textual root of takfir lies in the hadith literature, which contains extensive fabrications, whereas the Qur'an speaks in the language of the unified community (umma) and peaceful difference.
Al-Haydari rejects the traditional division of the world into the Domain of Islam (dar al-islam) and the Domain of War (dar al-harb), advocating instead for a modern framework of global peace.
The multiplicity of readings is an inevitable consequence of human reason and language, and it should serve as a tool for mutual integration rather than violent exclusion.
